nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: White mullet
Scientific Name: Mugil curema

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthyes
      Order: Perciformes
      Family: Mugilidae

Other Common Names: Silver mullet

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Valenciennes 1836)
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: Commonly consumed for food throughout its range (Cervigon 1966). Commercially valuable fish in Puerto Rico (Austin 1971). In Florida, it is also caught and sold as bait ‘finger mullet’. The white mullet bait fishery helps support a multi-million dollar sport fishery and related supply businesses (Nickerson 1984). Usually caught in a gill net or cast net.

Recreational: Used as bait ‘finger mullet’ in recreational fishery. Caught by recreational fisherman with cast nets for bait. The white mullet bait fishery helps support a multi-million dollar sport fishery and related supply businesses (Nickerson 1984).

Ecological Role: Abundant primary consumer in Indian River Lagoon and adjacent continental shelf, whose trophic position in the food web acts as a major mover of energy to higher trophic levels.  Mugil curerna is a very common fish found in inshore waters and is an important source of forage for large piscine and avian predators, and even some invertebrates (Gilmore and Gore 1974; Nickerson 1984; Gilmore 1988).

Indicator: As a benthic consumer and detritivore this species is more likely to consume and concentrate sediment contaminants, particularly those associated with organic molecules.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Mugil curema is found in the Atlantic from Massachusetts to Brazil and the western coast of Africa. It is also found in the eastern Pacific from California to Chile (Martin and Drewry 1978). Found along both coasts of Florida, however, it is more abundant on the Florida east coast (Springer and Woodburn 1960)

Within Study Area: Found throughout the Indian River Lagoon and adjacent marginal wetlands (Gilmore et al. 1982; Mulligan 1981; Gilmore 1988; Brown-Peterson and Eames 1990)

Mobility and Migration: Adult Mugil curema move to offshore continental shelf waters for spawning. Larvae are transported from this offshore pelagic habitat toward the coast. Prejuveniles Mugil curema move into estuaries particularly shallow seagrass meadows and wetlands. After maturation they then move into the more open estuarine waters of these habitat areas. Warm temperate populations migrate south in coastal waters during the winter. These winter movements can also take place in the warmer regions but on a smaller scale (Martin and Drewry 1978).

Life Mode: Mugil curema is a euryecious and euryhaline species that is found as planktonic larvae in continental shelf waters to 914 m (Collins and Stender 1989). Prejuvenile stage has been grouped into a category along with other prejuvenile mullet species called ‘querimana’ (Hoese and Moore 1977). During this stage the prejuveniles move toward the coast and shallow water habitats. The juveniles and adults are found in coastal waters, wetland habitats within estuaries.

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body: Habitat Type: Adults are found in coastal and estuarine waters including seagrass meadows, wetlands and freshwater (McLane 1955; Martin and Drewry 1978; Gilmore 1988). In tropical region M. curema is associated with mud substrate and turbid waters, or in clear water associated with sandy bottom and rocky areas (Cervigon 1966; Martin and Drewry 1978). Pelagic larvae are found in surface waters over the continental shelf out to the 914 m depth zone (Collins and Stender 1989). Prejuveniles are pelagic and marine with a migration to inshore waters. The juveniles move into the shallow coastal waters and wetland habitats in estuaries with mud bottom in the more tropical areas (Cervigon 1966; Martin and Drewry 1978). In the Indian River Lagoon adults, juveniles and prejuveniles of M. curema are found to associate with seagrasses (Gilmore 1988) and wetlands, including impounded salt marsh and mangrove habitats (Gilmore 1987; Gilmore et al. 1982).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: Mugil curema is a euryhaline species with a salinity range of 0-50 ppt. Since M. curema are found in marine, estuarine and freshwater habitats where salinities are variable, salinity tolerance is not a limiting factor in distribution (Martin and Drewry 198). Even though Mugil curema can tolerate low salinities it is usually found in saltier water than the striped mullet, Mugil cephalus.

Temperature:  may play an important role in distribution of Mugil curema. Low temperatures of 10 - 12.5 C have been attributed to cold kills in Texas (Martin and Drewry 1978). Low temperatures in all location may be a factor in winter migration. High temperatures do not appear to be a factor, with temperatures of 39 C being recorded for prejuveniles (Martin and Drewry 1978).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, external fertilization, iteroparous, broadcast spawner.

Spawning Strategy: Spawning takes place over continental shelf waters and surface waters over depths up to 914 m (Collins and Stender 1989). March to September with peaks in spring (Martin and Drewry 1978). However, Herrema et a1 (1985) considers Mugil curema a year-round spawner along the east coast of Florida.  Temperature above 20 C is suggested to trigger spawning (Martin and Drewry 1978).

Fecundity: No information available.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Unfertilized eggs are opaque with a diameter range 0.77-0.86 mm. Fertilized eggs are pelagic with a diameter of 0.86-0.92 mm two hours after fertilization. Egg contains a single oil globule. Hatching occurs in 42 hours (Martin and Drewry 1978).

Larvae: The larvae hatch at 1.63-1.76 mm TL (Martin and Drewry 1978). Feeding starts 35-40 h after hatching while 25 % of the yolk-sac is still present). Yolk-Sac absorption takes up to 3.5 days after hatching with the oil globule present until 6 days (Houde et al. 1976).

Juvenile: Prejuvenile stage ranges from 7.2-40 mm SL, and juvenile stage from 30-175 mm SL (Martin and Drewry 1978). Houde et al. (1976) considers the juvenile stage to start on cultured specimens at 5.5-6.5 mm SL (12-16 days post hatch) and therefore does not differentiate a prejuvenile stage. Growth has been estimated at 17 mm SL per month for the first year (Martin and Drewry 1978) or 0.56 mm per day (Houde et al. 1976).

Adult: Maturity may be reached in the first year. Males mature between 86 - 251 mm SL, average size, 189 mm SL. The females mature in a range from 90-251 mm SL, average size, 209 mm SL (Martin and Drewry 1978).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Mullets in general feed on detritus and plant material by grubbing through bottom sediments and on microorganisms adhering to plants and surface film (Odum 1966; Bohlke and Chaplin 1968; Robins et a1. 1986). Vieira (1991) used the term ‘iliophagous’ - combination of benthic microorganisms, detrital material and inorganic sediment to describe the diet of Mugil curema. The feeding behavior involves gulping sediment and spitting out the coarser particles and digesting the nutrient material. Mullet have a gizzard like stomach and exceedingly long intestines (Bohlke and Chaplin 1968). The juvenile Mugil curema is a planktivore with the diet consisting of; Diatoms, Cyanophyta, Dinoflagellates, Chlorophyceace, silicoflagellates, Crustaceans, and mineral particles (Vieira 1991)

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Mugil curema is a keystone species in the Indian River Lagoon. Filling many important roles in the complex food web and energy transport cycle, acting as a primary consumer, a mode of energy transport from wetlands and as prey source for aquatic predators (fishes, birds, marine mammals). Loss of habitats, such as seagrasses and wetlands, can have a marked impact on populations.

Low temperatures in all location may be a factor in winter migration. High temperatures do not appear to be a factor, with temperatures of 39 C being recorded for prejuveniles (Martin and Drewry 1978).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, external fertilization, iteroparous, broadcast spawner.

Spawning Strategy: Spawning takes place over continental shelf waters and surface waters over depths up to 914 m (Collins and Stender 1989). March to September with peaks in spring (Martin and Drewry 1978). However, Herrema et a1 (1985) considers Mugil curema a year-round spawner along the east coast of Florida.  Temperature above 20 C is suggested to trigger spawning (Martin and Drewry 1978).

Fecundity: No information available.

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Unfertilized eggs are opaque with a diameter range 0.77-0.86 mm. Fertilized eggs are pelagic with a diameter of 0.86-0.92 mm two hours after fertilization. Egg contains a single oil globule. Hatching occurs in 42 hours (Martin and Drewry 1978).

Larvae: The larvae hatch at 1.63-1.76 mm TL (Martin and Drewry 1978). Feeding starts 35-40 h after hatching while 25 % of the yolk-sac is still present). Yolk-Sac absorption takes up to 3.5 days after hatching with the oil globule present until 6 days (Houde et al. 1976).

Juvenile: Prejuvenile stage ranges from 7.2-40 mm SL, and juvenile stage from 30-175 mm SL (Martin and Drewry 1978). Houde et al. (1976) considers the juvenile stage to start on cultured specimens at 5.5-6.5 mm SL (12-16 days post hatch) and therefore does not differentiate a prejuvenile stage. Growth has been estimated at 17 mm SL per month for the first year (Martin and Drewry 1978) or 0.56 mm per day (Houde et al. 1976).

Adult: Maturity may be reached in the first year. Males mature between 86 - 251 mm SL, average size, 189 mm SL. The females mature in a range from 90-251 mm SL, average size, 209 mm SL (Martin and Drewry 1978).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Mullets in general feed on detritus and plant material by grubbing through bottom sediments and on microorganisms adhering to plants and surface film (Odum 1966; Bohlke and Chaplin 1968; Robins et a1. 1986). Vieira (1991) used the term ‘iliophagous’ - combination of benthic microorganisms, detrital material and inorganic sediment to describe the diet of Mugil curema. The feeding behavior involves gulping sediment and spitting out the coarser particles and digesting the nutrient material. Mullet have a gizzard like stomach and exceedingly long intestines (Bohlke and Chaplin 1968). The juvenile Mugil curema is a planktivore with the diet consisting of; Diatoms, Cyanophyta, Dinoflagellates, Chlorophyceace, silicoflagellates, Crustaceans, and mineral particles (Vieira 1991)

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: Mugil curema is a keystone species in the Indian River Lagoon. Filling many important roles in the complex food web and energy transport cycle, acting as a primary consumer, a mode of energy transport from wetlands and as prey source for aquatic predators (fishes, birds, marine mammals). Loss of habitats, such as seagrasses and wetlands, can have a marked impact on populations.
